claims.text: A combined high-throughput experimental and computational approach can determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a wide range of HEAs.
Electrostatic levitation and rapid DSC, combined with ab initio molecular dynamics and CALPHAD, provide accurate and efficient measurements across wide HEA compositional space.
Arc melting followed by prolonged homogenization can produce a uniform, single-phase HEA microstructure suitable for the measurements.
Containerless melting under high vacuum or inert gas minimizes sample contamination and interface effects.
High-vacuum or inert-gas conditions prevent oxidation during melting and phase-change experiments.
DSC heating rates of approximately 100–200 K/s can accurately capture dynamic melting in HEAs.
A homogenized, single-phase solid solution causes measured latent thermal properties to reflect intrinsic HEA behavior rather than microsegregation or secondary-phase effects.
Electrostatic levitation and rapid calorimetry provide fast and accurate capture of thermal transitions.
Free-energy landscapes computed by ab initio molecular dynamics for liquid and solid phases can pinpoint melting transitions and associated latent thermal properties.
CALPHAD calibration anchored to known binary or ternary systems improves predictions for multicomponent HEAs.
The proposed approach will determine HEA melting temperatures to within ±1–2% of conventional benchmarks.
The proposed approach will determine fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting to within ±5% of conventional benchmarks.
The proposed approach will determine liquid density and heat capacity with high fidelity across compositional ranges covering most conventional HEAs.
Traditional slower DSC or DTA measurements have higher uncertainty than the proposed approach.
Estimates extrapolated from binary phase diagrams have limited transferability to multielement HEAs.
The methodology is less effective for HEAs with significant evaporation, high-temperature reactivity, or persistent microstructural inhomogeneity.
Performance varies with alloy system and processing history.
Calibration against well-characterized reference alloys is necessary.
Ab initio prediction uncertainties for multicomponent alloys may exceed those for simpler alloys.

Consistent deviations greater than 5% from established benchmarks, or failure of independent experiments and simulations to converge for a statistically significant HEA set, would render the approach inadequate.
